lesson.title: ASCII and Unicode: From English Letters to Every Written Language
lesson.summary: Contrasts ASCII, a 7-bit encoding limited to 128 English oriented characters, with Unicode and its common UTF-8 encoding, which represents virtually every character in every writing system.
lesson.body:
ASCII, short for American Standard Code for Information Interchange, was one of the earliest widely adopted character encoding standards, developed in the 1960s. It assigns a numeric code to each of 128 characters using just 7 bits, which comfortably fits within a single 8 bit byte with one bit to spare. Those 128 characters cover uppercase and lowercase English letters, the digits 0 through 9, common punctuation, and a handful of control characters used for things like line breaks. The example from the previous section, where ord('A') returned 65, is describing an ASCII code point directly, since 65 is A's position within the ASCII standard.

ASCII worked well for English language text on early computers, but its limitation is obvious once you consider the rest of the world's writing systems. With only 128 available codes, ASCII has no way to represent accented letters like e with an acute accent or n with a tilde, no way to represent non Latin alphabets like Cyrillic or Greek, and absolutely no way to represent character based writing systems like Chinese, which alone has thousands of distinct characters in common use. As computing became global, this limitation became a real problem, not just an inconvenience.

Unicode was created to solve this problem completely. Rather than assigning codes to only 128 characters, Unicode assigns a unique number, called a code point, to essentially every character used in every major writing system in the world, along with symbols, emoji, and more. Critically, Unicode's first 128 code points are defined to exactly match ASCII, so any valid ASCII text is automatically valid under Unicode as well, with the very same numeric codes.

Having a code point number for a character is only half the story. That number still needs to be turned into actual bytes to be stored or transmitted, and the most widely used scheme for doing this is called UTF-8. UTF-8 is a variable width encoding: characters that match the original ASCII range use exactly 1 byte, exactly as before, while characters outside that range use 2, 3, or 4 bytes, depending on how large their code point number is. This is visible directly in Python:

word = "caf\u00e9"
print(len(word))
print(len(word.encode('utf-8')))

The first print statement outputs 4, because the word is made of four characters: c, a, f, and the accented e. The second print statement outputs 5, because when encoded into UTF-8 bytes, the letters c, a, and f each take a single byte, but the accented e, which lies outside the original ASCII range, requires 2 bytes to represent in UTF-8. This gap, between the number of characters and the number of bytes needed to store them, is exactly the distinction between a Unicode code point and its UTF-8 encoding, and it is why modern software must be careful to specify which encoding it is using whenever it reads or writes text.
